sentences.text: Hi Andy.
This meeting is being recorded.
Hello, Andy.
How you doing?
I'm alright, thanks.
How are you doing?
Yeah, not too bad.
Sorry about that.
Postman at the front door and the dog going crazy just as you, you entered the room.
Perfect timing.
I set it all up.
Oh, who's Dave?
Is he with you?
Yes, he's group cfo.
Okay, Dave's entering the room.
You've been up to what we've been up to.
We.
We bought a renewables business in March and it is taking every waking second and most of the sleeping ones.
So that's sort of been up to.
Yeah.
So what's that?
It's some kind of energy thing?
Yeah, Heat pumps, solar batteries, MVHR air conditioning.
Mostly high end residential in London and southeast.
Completely different space.
Yeah, sounds.
Sounds exciting.
How can you get into that then?
That's a good question.
So having.
Having run Exposure Ninja for a bit, I just, I got a bit bored and put the CEO charge.
That was November 2023.
Always wanted to sort of buy some of our clients really and choose an industry that we thought had a bit of.
A bit of potential, a bit of tailwind.
So we identified renewables as one and then bought half of an insulation installer last year.
It was a bit small, bit of a waste of time to be honest, so it went a bit bigger with this one.
And yeah, it's been really good fun.
Really, really good fun.
A lot of work, but yeah, sounds great.
Well, congratulations anyway.
All right, so.
So you're thinking of selling Exposure Ninja, is it?
Yeah, yeah.
Because as more of my, my time has been spent.
Dave's group cfo.
So Dave's at the holding company.
Sorry.
Yeah.
Good to see you.
Right.
It's his birthday today, so we're being really nice.
Happy birthday.
Yeah.
Andy.
We normally do a thing where we sing to him at the start of every meeting, so it's yours.
Please don't.
Yeah, the most awkward thing in the world, isn't it?

But yeah, with more time being spent on the renewable stuff and Exposure Ninja being completely self sufficient, the only time I spend on it is half a day a week for making a video for the YouTube channel.
If we had cash up front in a deal, a component of cash upfront, we could invest in a renewables business and go a lot harder and faster with it.
So that's the reason really, Exposure Ninjas on the up.
It's just had its best quarter ever.
Best half year ever, just had its best month ever.
It's well positioned for AI.
We're pioneers in AI search optimization and we're getting a lot of inquiries around that.
So I thought seems like a good time and it'll allow us to go harder and faster with renewables.
Yeah, okay, brilliant.
All right.
Well, yeah, I mean it is a good time at the moment.
The market seems very buoyant.
We're seeing a lot of activity on both sides.
Obviously we work on the buy and the sell side, but yeah, we've never been busier on the sell side really.
I think we've got about four or five Lois on the table at the moment with clients.
So yeah, it's really, it's really popping at the moment.
So whereabouts is the business?
So you're not involved in it at all, Tim.
And who is the sort of leadership of the agency on a day to day basis?
Yeah, so there's a CEO who's been with us for 11 years, a COO who's also been with us for 11 years, Director of People, director of Finance, Sales Director.
Wow.
They're the senior leadership team and then there's a management layer underneath those individual managers of each department and it's completely remote.
Sorry, sorry.
What is the size of the business?
What's the revenue be?
About 4 million this year with 800k EBITDA.
So it's a really, you could say well built or you could say overbuilt structure for its size, but we've always sort of done that.
We've always invested in the infrastructure first and then sort of grown into the revenue.
So.
Right, so I mean, that sounds perfect.
Are you in a perfect position really to.
To sell it on?
I mean most buyers would die for that sort of infrastructure and team structure on something that they acquire.
So that's really interesting.
And what are you looking for, for it?
What, what are you looking to do?
Have you got any ideas?
Not really, to be honest.
Maximum cash up front is the goal because then we can invest it like it's doing well, it's stable, it doesn't need me.
So if it was like a, you know, typical mainly earnout type thing, may as well just hold it.
So the whole point of this is to free up as much cash as possible.
Dave's going to make sure I don't undersell it because my tendency is I'm already sort of mentally moved on.
But those much more, that's good to.
Hold the line for me.
And so Dave, what, what are you thinking?
What are you seeing in the market that you want to sort of replicate in terms of valuation?
Yeah, I mean I'm.
I'M sort of around the 5 million mark.
I'm seeing everything trending upwards.
As Tim said, best month, best quarter, best half.
There's absolutely no signals to me that suggest that that isn't a trend that's here to stay, given that we're right.
So I use this analogy.
I hate analogies, but sort of riding the start of what will become a tidal wave, we're sort of.
We've got on at the right point, we're further ahead of the field and all of the inquiries are coming in and all the performances there.
The 800,000 EBITDA is a very realistic and actually in some senses maybe even conservative for.
For the year.
That's just based on replicating what we've done in the first half, when really it's probably going to be slightly bigger than that.
So I am still sort of taking the lower end and then just sort of.
You're looking at the 4 to 6 sort of multiplier valuation range.
Let's take 5 as the midpoint and go for 4 million.
Something in the 4 to 5 million range.
4 to 5 million.
Okay.
Yeah.
So I would.
I would agree something in the.
Around 4 would.
Would possibly be about right.
I would say a 5x for a good, solid, healthy business like that is.
Is pretty good.
Could we get over that?
I think.
I think most buyers would feel that they were overpaying if it was 6.7x for.
For the business, just purely on the size, but we haven't really looked into the business yet.
It could be that, you know, if you've got absolutely everything clean as a whistle and it's just growing and there's more.
More coming in.
What.
What was the full year EBITDA for the last full financial year that you had.
The last full year was.
Sorry, I looked at that the other day.
Did we say it was 550 last.
Last.
Last year, Tim?
I think it's just a bit over 500.
550, something like that.
Yeah.
But we've done 400 already this year, haven't we?
Yeah.
And how much have you got left?
The financial year.
Calendar.
Calendar year.
It's a calendar year.
Yeah.
Okay.
Actually, the timing's quite good, then.
Okay, that sounds all right.
All right.
So.
So you're saying.
Yeah, we did exactly.
I think pretty much bang on 400 the first six months of the year.
Okay.
And what was the previous year?
I mean, there's obviously going to be a trend of it going up.
I think that there's a danger to sort of over egg the pudding a little bit because obviously that's the current year and there is a bit of a difference between 550 and 800.
Yes, absolutely.
We're definitely trending up.
Let me get the numbers.
400, I want to say.
Yeah, so on EBITDA basis.
So that's what that would be the calendar year.
Yeah, calendar year.
So, yeah, that's it for.
Yeah, just over 500 last year.
Just over 400 the year before.
372 before that.
Yeah.
Okay.
All right.
So I would say we're probably on a solid 5x.
So let's see where we're at at the point when somebody makes an offer.
But we could go for around 5x and 4 million.
I think given that you're not quite there, I think that would be more realistic than.
Yeah, sounds good.
One of the things Tim's mentioned earlier today as well is obviously the goal is cash up front.
So we're not overly interested in an earn out because if we were interested in that, we'd just keep hold of the business and just wait for the profit to come in.
Obviously that has the knock on effect on the ultimate valuation.
So just.
Yeah, we're aware of that.
The difficulty that you've got in the UK is that the buyer would have to have all the money to pay it up front because we don't have SBA lenders in the uk.
In America you can get slightly better cash upfront deals.
We're actually selling the company at the moment with I think around 1995 cash up front.
But in the UK, those types of deals are extremely rare.
Not to say they never happen, but it's very, very unlikely that somebody would offer all cash up front.
Yeah, definitely not expecting all cash up front.
The other thing probably worth mentioning is about half our revenue is us.
So.
It'S the buyer though.
So.
Yeah, I mean, it still could be an American buyer, but they wouldn't be able to use SBA loans to buy a company outside of the us.
Are you structured in.
In the uk?
We are, yeah, yeah, yeah.
So.
So most likely would still, even if it was an American buyer, they would probably structure it the same with.
With half cash on day one and then it would be an earn out.
So, yeah, Dave, I would just say it's so typical of the deal structure for service businesses that we're unlikely to be able to.
To avoid it.
Even if we pushed for more cash upfront, there would be very few people that could close it with.
In a cash deal.
Yeah, yeah, no, that's Fine.
It's more just sort of setting out the sort of initial stall of this is where we're benchmarked.
Well aware that those things change as you actually go out to market.
I think possibly the, the best case scenario is we, we push for a really, really short earn out.
We, we did sell a, a company in Austin, Texas that had a 12 month earn out and they actually just hit the target in nine months.
And so they got all of their cash out of the business at month nine.
And they were in a similar position as you Tim.
They had built a very sort of management heavy team anyway and the founder and the CFO had built a software business on the side.
And so they just wanted to get out and they did it extremely quickly.

So I think maybe our best option would, would still be, it would still be just because of the way the businesses work, some kind of earn out but we could stick with the earn out as a short period of time as possible.
But really the difficulty we have is just the way that deals are funded.
They're funded by the business that they buy.

And just because service businesses are so it doesn't sound like this businesses, but service businesses are so easy to sort of push over that the buyers tend to just have lots of caveats in the deal that makes it really, really safe for them to take over the business.
So I mean the ideal scenario would be I would say is probably like a 5x or maybe a bit more with a 12 month earn out.
But it could be that the buyers will.
It doesn't matter what you put on the table really.
It's something that everybody can do and we need to find a good buyer with the cash that you're happy with selling to.

And you know, we need to find culture fit and there's so many other things at the time, you know, when we've got buyers at the table that we, we're trying to get, you know, as many ticks in the boxes as possible.
It's not usually, you know, just give it to anybody who's offering cash even.
Yeah, yeah.
So, but okay, but I think in principle you're kind of there, you're not being overly unreasonable.
I would say a 5.5X is pretty solid.
But let's take a look at the, the books and see where you are and yeah, certainly we would be, we would be happy to, to take something that was reasonably priced to market.
So are you aware of, of how we, we work?
I'm, I can talk you through.
Yeah, I've looked at some of your deals as a buyer, but I don't know how you work as a seller.
Oh yeah, totally different.
No, I would always, I would always suggest whichever side of the fence that you're on, that you have an advisory going to market or at least a go to market plan.
But, but basically the way we work.
So we've got a couple of different tiers that would, would work for you just due to your size and the, is the sense of urgency really.
So, so I'll give you both these price in dollars.
So we've got the platinum process, which is the full M and a process.
So this is like a, a guaranteed approach of getting your business sold.
It's not guaranteed to be sold within six months, but it's pretty much guaranteed.
The process is a six month process to get the business sold.
And the difference with this versus everything else that we do is that we are, we're working on this deal every single day going out to market until we get a buyer, until we get the deal closed.
Now sometimes it takes a bit longer than six months, but the process is really solid.
And usually I would say within the first two or three months we do have very strong engagement with buyers.
Are you guys there?
Yep, yep, still here.
We have very similar engagement with buyers right from the, the off really.
So it takes about three or four weeks to get up and running and set up.
But usually, you know, within the first two or three months we, we've got strong engagement with a buyer that's really interested.
And so then it's just a process of going through the buyers getting a good offer on the table, usually leveraging one against the other.
So we'll set like a date in the, you know, a date in a flag in the ground of where we want offers to come in at.
And so we tend to have sort of two or three, sometimes much more.
We've had situation where we've had sort of like 40 or 50 signed NDAs and sort of five or six offers on the table at the same time.
So the ideal situation is to have two or three really so you can leverage one against the other.
Usually one of those will be a really good buyer that you can get a deal done with.
And then it's a case of due diligence, then the legal negotiation as well, once we've got everything agreed and then that.
So that whole process usually takes somewhere between 30 to 90 days to get done.

So even on a relatively small business, it will still take sort of 30, 30 or so days to do due diligence and a Slightly large business like what you have, even with clean books it can just run a bit longer, but there is usually a 90 day period.
So that kind of pushes out the sort of three or four months of actually talking to buyers onto a sort of six month timeline to get the deal done.
Yep.
Which is unfortunate because we're in July.
One of the nice things about going into the second half of the year is that actually people just want to get the deal done by Christmas.
So sometimes everything just zips along through December and just gets, gets closed.
I don't mess around in due diligence either.
We'll be all over that.
When you've got a clean set of books and a good team as well, everything just gets delivered up, which just makes it really, really quick.
We're in the same process actually.
We've got a husband and wife team in New York and the wife is, her books are just clean as a whistle and she's just churning out stuff.
Every time they ask for something new it's just getting sent out extremely quickly.
So yeah, that's good to know.
But that's the one thing that really holds things up once we go in.
In fact, the, anything that holds up the process even by a day or two can actually just push the deal over.
You know, everybody is emotional.
Buyers are emotional as well and they get really pissed off if people aren't responding really quickly.
So.
But yeah, anyway, so that's, that's like the full process, that's $30,000.
So it's a ten thousand dollar deposit or eight thousand pounds.
And then the rest of the payments are broken up over the next four months.
But that kind of guarantees this six month process and that we're, we're working on this deal every single day to get the deal done.
There's a slightly sort of cut down version for sellers that are not as desperate to get a deal done, which is 10,750.
And the difference with this really is that we're prepping the business to go to market.
So we're doing the same sort of starting phase.
So we're digging into your books, doing a full valuation.
So we'll come back to you and give you like an evaluation range.

After going through your books, we build out all of the marketing materials so your sim, the teaser and the listing and that goes out to our network and it goes out to a sort of bespoke list of buyers that we initially do.
Then after that we're not pushing these deals to get closed every single day, but we are pushing them to get closed.

I've just said like two or three deals actually that we have at the moment that are in the gold package, which is this one, are moving towards close right now and they are where we've had sort of gaps, where we haven't had the interest every single day because we're not sort of pumping it every day.
But we're still out looking for buyers.
It's still marketed on our mailing list and on the Agencies Co website as well.
So it's still a pretty solid approach but it's is there is less urgency to get the deal done.
So it really depends, you know, what, what your approach is right now.
So do those both make.
Make sense?
Yes.
Yep.
Yeah.
Cool.
All right, so I can put those in an email.
They're also on the Agencies Co pricing page as well, which kind of explains the process quite clearly.
But I'll send those over on an email.
If you guys need a bit of time to talk about it, then we can, maybe we can follow up next week.
Yeah, sounds good.
Andy, what would you say your success rate is on each of them and I guess just in general?
Yeah, our success rate is, and I hate saying our success rates because it sounds quite low, but it's around the 30% mark.
But actually it is, it is quite good.
Now the, one of the reasons why I'm proud of our success rate is we do actually close most of the deals for sellers who are engaged in the process.
We do have a very low tier where you can just come in and get your business valued and listed on agencies and some people are just testing the market, they want to see if there's any interest.
And then there is about a third of our clients, I would say very roughly about a third who are very emotional coming into the process.
They don't really know what their company's worth.
We have to, we always do a sort of full valuation process at the start to sort of lay out why we feel the value is what it is.
But we are comparing prices in the market.
But, but some people just can't, they can't accept that.
So they will go to market.
Silly multiples.
I mean, we've got a client at the moment that's on there for 7x and the business is worth a 3 and a half, 4x which we're getting offers at.
But we are still, we're not, we're still not closed because they're not accepting anything that is.
Isn't where they want it.
And this isn't a professional company.
Was as well, with the board and investors, but yeah, I mean some prices we just can't get no matter how, how good we are.
So, so I'd say it's, it is, it's around 30, but it's actually a pretty good rate even in the industry.
I think it's 1 in 10 or something then.
So it, it's pretty good.
Yeah, I know like shop shops like KBS would die for 30% when they.
Yeah, probably.
Yeah, well, exactly.
Again they're just listing people that probably just don't understand anything to do with it at all and they've got no chance of, of, of closing the deal.
I think the other thing to remember is, you know, we are experts in this domain and we have a lot of traffic.
I mean we're, we're, we have like the same people over and over and over and over again like signing NDAs.
They're desperate to buy a marketing agency on the site.
So we're extremely busy and we have a lot of exposure.
I mean if you are a marketing agency and you look to sell, particularly in the uk, I would say we're pretty much number one in terms of exposure.
Yeah.
Okay, great.
Thanks Andy.
Really useful.
I don't think I've got any other questions.
Have you got anything, Dave?
Yeah, are there any other fees we need to be aware of?
So we, we charge a 5% win fee when we get the deal closed, but that's net of anything that you paid as in retainers up until that point.
So yeah, there, there is the win fee.
Yeah, a big piece, piece of the pie.
And that's the same on.
No matter which process or route you go down with you guys, it's 5%.
It's always 5%.
Yeah, I mean we've got some, some companies that are just really tiny and we list them for free and we still, we still take like a minimum win fee.
So.
Yeah.
And is that on total deal size or is it just the cash up front?
Like is there any.
How's it going?
It's on the whole deal.
So some M and A companies actually structure it differently and we'll charge like a 10% win fee and they take 10% of cash, but we actually take 5% on all cash as it comes through the deal.
So I mean some deals we've got like a five year wait to get all of the cash out of it, but we, we take the money as the, as the seller take, you know, gets the money.
So that's how we work.
Okay, cool.
Good stuff.
Yep.
Okay, cool.
All right.
I'll put everything in, in an email and fire over.
Was there anything else?
I mean, I'm really looking forward to working with, with you, Tim.
I think this is a high quality business for us.

You know, the best thing is to, to, to, to get great businesses through because like I say, we get so much, so many buyers that just want to get a deal done that when we go to market with something like this, the, the likelihood of getting a deal done quite quickly is, is really high.
So.
Okay, cool.
Yeah, that sounds good.
Looking forward to, to seeing a thing that you're sending and we'll take it from there then.
Okay, perfect.
All right, good stuff, guys.
Good to see you.
Thanks.
Good to me, Andy.
Yeah, nice to meet you as well, Dave.
Speak soon.

summary.overview:
- Tim Cameron-Kitchen's business focus shifted to renewables after purchase in March 2024, with products like heat pumps and solar batteries targeting high-end residential in London/Southeast.  
- Exposure Ninja's leadership structure remains strong, with the CEO and COO both having 11 years of tenure, ensuring stability and operational expertise.  
- Projected revenue for 2024 stands at £4 million with an £800k EBITDA, highlighting robust financial health despite a complete remote operation.  
- Dave estimates the business valuation between £4-5 million, applying a 5x multiplier based on the current performance trajectory.  
- Andy concurs with the 5x multiplier for valuation but warns against overpricing at 6-7x for the business size.  
- Cash preference is paramount for Tim, with a clear priority for maximum upfront payment over an earnout structure, even if it affects valuation.  
- UK market constraints identified, including the absence of SBA lending, making all-cash deals rare compared to the US market.  
- Typical deal structure involves 50% cash on day one and earnout for the remainder, with recommendations for a 12-month earnout as an optimal solution.  
- Service process includes platinum and gold package options, with success rates described as 30% overall but higher for engaged sellers.  
- Fee structure is clarified as a 5% commission on total deal value received by the seller, net of retainer payments.
summary.short_summary: Tim Cameron-Kitchen has shifted his business focus to renewable energy products such as heat pumps and solar batteries, particularly targeting high-end residential markets in London and the Southeast. Exposure Ninja benefits from strong leadership with both the CEO and COO having 11 years of experience, ensuring operational stability. The projected revenue for 2024 is £4 million, with an EBITDA of £800k, demonstrating solid financial health despite operating entirely remotely. Business valuation is estimated between £4-5 million, with a 5x multiplier applied, though there are cautions against overpricing. Tim prefers cash transactions, prioritizing upfront payment over earnout options, which is influenced by UK market constraints. The typical deal structure involves 50% cash on the first day, with a recommended 12-month earnout. Service offerings include platinum and gold packages, with a commission structure of 5% on total deal value net of retainers.
